title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about research at university: what academic research actually is, and how a research project is shaped before anyone runs it. By the end you will be able to explain what makes work count as research, describe how a research proposal shapes a project, and recognise the main parts of a research project.

Research is not just looking things up. It is how knowledge is made and tested in every subject, and at some point your degree will ask you to do it, often in a dissertation. Knowing what research is, and how a project is built, makes that moment far less daunting.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what academic research is and what makes a piece of work count as research
describe how a research project is shaped by a research proposal and its guiding questions
recognise the main parts of a research project and how they fit together.

title: In real academic practice
body: Research underpins your whole degree. Every reading list points to research others have done, every dissertation asks you to do some of your own, and the judgement research demands, asking good questions and weighing evidence, is prized in professional work too. Understanding what research is now gives you a head start when a project lands on your desk.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what academic research is: how it differs from simply gathering information. Second, shaping a project: how a research proposal and its questions build the framework for a study. Third, the shape of a research project: the parts that carry it from question to findings. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You have probably been told to 'do some research' for an assignment and taken it to mean looking things up. Academic research means something more particular. This lesson is about what research actually is at university, so that when your course asks you to do research, or to read it, you know what the word is really asking for.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies, and you may not have run a research project yet. You are not expected to design a study or write a dissertation at this stage. The aim is to recognise what makes work count as research and to see how an extended project such as a dissertation fits together.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what makes a piece of work count as research rather than a summary of sources
recognise research rather than summary in a worked example of two students' approaches
identify what counts as research when you meet it in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Academic research is systematic inquiry: you ask a focused question, gather evidence in a planned way, and reach a conclusion you can defend. What makes it research is not the topic but the move from a question to a reasoned answer. A piece that only gathers and reports what others have said is a summary; research uses those sources to build something of its own.

Research also aims at a fresh perspective. It need not be wholly original, in the sense of never done before. More often it brings a new angle, a new case or a new combination to an existing conversation. The dissertation is the fullest example you will meet: an extended piece of research that draws on all your academic literacies on a grander scale.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The key idea: research
body: Research is the word your course will use again and again. Reveal what it means at university.
instruction: Select to reveal the full definition.
definition: Systematic inquiry that asks a focused question, gathers evidence in a planned way, and reaches a conclusion you can defend.
extendedDefinition: Academic research is more than looking things up. It uses sources to build something of its own and aims at a fresh perspective, a new angle or case brought to an existing conversation, rather than wholly original work.
example: A student who asks a clear question, gathers evidence to answer it, and reaches a defensible conclusion is doing research; one who only reports what others said is summarising.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Consider two students asked to produce a short research piece using the same set of sources.

{{learner-a}} reads the sources, picks out what each one says, and writes them up one after another: this author found this, that author found that. The work is accurate and tidy. But it only gathers and reports; it asks no question of its own and reaches no conclusion. This is a summary, not research.

{{learner-b}} starts from a focused question, then uses the same sources as evidence towards answering it. The sources are weighed, connected, and brought to bear on a conclusion {{learner-b}} can defend. A fresh angle emerges that none of the sources stated alone. This is research.

Both students used the same sources. Only {{learner-b}} turned them into an inquiry with a question and a defensible answer.

title: Research habits
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These checks help you tell research from summary in your own work. Try them on your next assignment.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I asked a focused question, rather than just a topic to cover?
Am I using my sources as evidence towards an answer, not just reporting them?
Have I connected the sources to each other, rather than listing them one by one?
Does my work reach a conclusion I could defend with reasons?
Have I brought a fresh angle, case or combination, rather than repeating what the sources say?
Could I explain, in one sentence, what my inquiry adds?

title: Formative check: what makes work research
displayTitle: Which of these best describes what makes a piece of work count as research rather than a summary?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What makes a piece of work count as research rather than a summary?

_items.text: It starts from a focused question and uses sources as evidence towards a defensible conclusion.
_items.feedback: Yes. A question answered with evidence is what turns sources into research.

_items.text: It gathers what several sources say and reports each one accurately.
_items.feedback: Accurate reporting of sources is a summary, not research.

_items.text: It uses more sources than a summary would.
_items.feedback: The number of sources is not what makes work research.

_items.text: It is written in formal, academic language.
_items.feedback: Formal language is a matter of style, not what makes work research.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Research starts from a focused question and uses sources as evidence towards a defensible conclusion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about a question answered with evidence, rather than reporting or style.
_incorrect.final: Research starts from a focused question and uses sources as evidence towards a conclusion. Reporting sources, counting them, or writing formally are not what make work research.

title: Formative check: research versus summary
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's work research rather than a summary?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's work research rather than a summary?

_items.text: They started from a focused question and used the sources as evidence towards a conclusion of their own.
_items.feedback: Yes. A question plus a defensible conclusion is the move from summary to research.

_items.text: They reported what each source said, one after another.
_items.feedback: Reporting each source in turn is exactly the summary the first student produced.

_items.text: They read the sources more carefully than the first student.
_items.feedback: Careful reading alone does not turn a summary into research.

_items.text: They used a longer list of sources than the first student.
_items.feedback: The length of the source list is not what made it research.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student asked a question and used the sources as evidence towards a conclusion of their own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID with the sources, beyond reading or listing them.
_incorrect.final: The second student's work was research because they asked a focused question and used the sources as evidence towards a defensible conclusion, not because they read more carefully or used more sources.

title: Formative check: research in your subject
displayTitle: You come across a piece of work in {{context}}. Which of these would count as research rather than summary?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which piece of work would count as research rather than summary?

_items.text: It poses a focused question and answers it with evidence, reaching a conclusion of its own.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, a question answered with evidence towards a conclusion is research.

_items.text: It gathers and reports what the main sources in {{context}} say on a topic.
_items.feedback: Gathering and reporting sources is a summary, even in {{context}}.

_items.text: It lists every source available on the topic in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: A list of sources is not research, however complete it is.

_items.text: It restates a well-known finding in {{context}} in clearer words.
_items.feedback: Restating a finding more clearly is description, not research.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, research poses a focused question and answers it with evidence towards a conclusion of its own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that asks a question and answers it with evidence, rather than gathering or restating.
_incorrect.final: In {{context}}, research poses a focused question and answers it with evidence towards a conclusion. Gathering, listing or restating sources is summary, not research.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Academic research is systematic inquiry: a focused question answered with evidence towards a defensible conclusion, aiming at a fresh perspective rather than a summary of sources. You can now explain what makes work count as research and recognise it when you see it. The dissertation is the fullest example, an extended project that draws on all your academic literacies. instruction: This lesson draws on the following sources.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw what makes work research. Before any research is done, though, the project has to be shaped: a vague interest has to become something you can actually carry out. This lesson is about how that shaping happens, through a research proposal, and why the proposal matters even for a small project.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to write a full research proposal yet. The aim is to understand what a proposal is for and how it turns an interest into a workable plan, so that when you meet one, as part of a dissertation or a module task, you know what it is asking you to do.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain the purpose of a research proposal in shaping a project
recognise how guiding questions build a project's framework
choose a guiding question that would help shape a project in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A research proposal is the plan you write before you begin: it sets out what you want to find out, why it is worth doing, and how you will go about it. Its job is to shape a project, turning a broad interest into a focused study with clear limits. A good proposal is what separates a vague idea from a project you can actually complete.

Proposals are often built from a series of carefully created questions. Working through them, what is my topic, what is already known, what gap or fresh angle am I pursuing, and how will I gather evidence, forces you to engage with the topic in a guided, structured way. Answering each question as fully as you can creates a framework for the whole project.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: How a project takes shape
body: A research project is shaped in stages, each one narrowing a broad interest into a workable plan.
instruction: Step through each stage to see how a project is shaped.

_items.title: A broad interest
_items.body: You start with something you find interesting but too big to study: a topic, not yet a project.

_items.title: A focused question
_items.body: Reading around the topic, you narrow it to a question you could actually answer, with clear limits on what you will and will not cover.

_items.title: A plan for evidence
_items.body: You decide what evidence would answer the question and how you would gather it, so the project becomes something you can carry out.

_items.title: A proposal
_items.body: The question, its justification and the plan come together as a proposal: the framework that guides the whole project from here.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students want to research the same broad area, and each writes a short proposal.

{{learner-a}} writes that the area is interesting and important, lists several things that could be looked at, and promises to read widely and report back. The proposal is enthusiastic, but it sets no focused question and no limits. With nothing to guide it, the project could go anywhere, and {{learner-a}} will struggle to know when it is finished.

{{learner-b}} works through a series of questions: what exactly do I want to find out, what is already known, what fresh angle am I taking, and how will I gather evidence? Each answer narrows the project. The result is one focused question with clear limits and a plan to match. The proposal has become a framework.

Both students began with the same interest. Only {{learner-b}} used guiding questions to shape it into a project that can actually be carried out.

title: Shaping questions
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These are the questions a proposal works through. Use them to turn an interest into a project.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Can I state, in one sentence, what I want to find out?
Have I checked what is already known about it?
Have I named the fresh angle, case or combination I am bringing?
Have I set clear limits on what the project will and will not cover?
Have I decided what evidence would answer my question?
Have I worked out how I would gather that evidence?

title: Formative check: the purpose of a proposal
displayTitle: What is the main purpose of a research proposal?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the main purpose of a research proposal?

_items.text: To shape a project: to turn a broad interest into a focused study with a plan you can carry out.
_items.feedback: Yes. A proposal shapes a project into something workable.

_items.text: To summarise everything already written about the topic.
_items.feedback: Summarising the existing writing is not the purpose of a proposal.

_items.text: To report the findings of the research once it is complete.
_items.feedback: Findings are reported later; a proposal comes before the research is done.

_items.text: To list as many possible questions about a topic as you can.
_items.feedback: A proposal focuses on one question, rather than listing many.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A proposal shapes a project, turning a broad interest into a focused study with a workable plan.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a proposal does before the research begins.
_incorrect.final: A proposal shapes a project into a focused study with a plan you can carry out. It does not summarise the literature, report findings, or list every possible question.

title: Formative check: guiding questions
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do that turned a broad interest into a workable project?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do that turned a broad interest into a workable project?

_items.text: Worked through guiding questions that narrowed the interest to one focused question with clear limits.
_items.feedback: Yes. Guiding questions did the shaping, building a framework for the project.

_items.text: Promised to read widely and report back on the whole area.
_items.feedback: That is what the first student did, and it set no focus or limits.

_items.text: Listed several things that could be looked at in the area.
_items.feedback: A list of possibilities is not a focused, workable project.

_items.text: Chose a topic that was more interesting than the first student's.
_items.feedback: Both students chose the same area; interest was not the difference.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student used guiding questions to narrow the interest into one focused question with clear limits.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that narrowed the interest and set limits, rather than widening it.
_incorrect.final: The second student worked through guiding questions that narrowed the interest to one focused question with clear limits. Reading widely or listing possibilities leaves the project unshaped.

title: Formative check: a guiding question
displayTitle: You are starting a small research project in {{context}}. Which of these is the best guiding question to help shape it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the best guiding question to help shape a project?

_items.text: A focused question, with clear limits, that you could actually answer with evidence in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Yes. A focused, answerable question is what shapes a project in {{context}}.

_items.text: A broad statement that the topic in {{context}} is interesting and important.
_items.feedback: A statement of interest is not a question and does not shape the project.

_items.text: A promise to read everything written about the topic in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Reading everything is neither focused nor a question.

_items.text: A list of every question that could possibly be asked in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: A long list widens the project instead of focusing it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a focused question with clear limits, answerable with evidence, is what shapes a project.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the focused, answerable question, rather than a statement, a promise or a long list.
_incorrect.final: In {{context}}, the best guiding question is focused, limited and answerable with evidence. A statement of interest, a promise to read everything, or a long list of questions all leave the project unshaped.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a topic in your subject you find interesting. What is one focused question you could ask about it, and what would you need to leave out to keep the project workable?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A research proposal shapes a project: it turns a broad interest into a focused study with a plan you can carry out. Built from a series of guiding questions, it becomes a framework for the whole project. You can now explain what a proposal is for and recognise how guiding questions do the shaping. The next lesson looks at the shape a project takes on the page.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

title: Orientation
body: You have seen what research is and how a project is shaped. This lesson looks at the shape a research project takes on the page. Most research write-ups, from a lab report to a dissertation, follow a recognisable pattern, and knowing the parts helps you read research and, later, write it.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to write a full report or dissertation yet. The aim is to recognise the main parts of a research project and see how each one does a particular job, so the overall structure makes sense when you meet it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise the core parts of a research write-up: introduction, methodology, results and discussion
identify which part of a project a piece of writing belongs to
match a stage of a research project in {{context}} to the part that reports it.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A research write-up has a recognisable shape, and in many subjects it follows four core parts. The introduction sets out the question and why it matters. The methodology explains how the research was done, so that someone else could judge or repeat it. The results report what was found, plainly. The discussion weighs what the findings mean and how far they answer the question.

These parts are not just a template. They carry the reader through the logic of the project, from the question, through how it was tackled, to what was found and what it means. In the sciences this is often called the report structure; a dissertation follows the same thread on a grander scale.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The parts of a research project
body: Four parts carry a research project from its question to what its findings mean. Review each card.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Introduction
_items.subtitle: The question
_items.text: Sets out what the project is asking and why it matters, placing it in the wider conversation.

_items.title: Methodology
_items.subtitle: The how
_items.text: Explains how the research was carried out, in enough detail that someone else could judge or repeat it.

_items.title: Results
_items.subtitle: The findings
_items.text: Reports what was found, plainly and without interpretation, so the evidence stands on its own.

_items.title: Discussion
_items.subtitle: The meaning
_items.text: Weighs what the findings mean, how far they answer the question, and what their limits are.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students write up the same small study, and we look at how each handles the parts.

{{learner-a}} opens by giving away the main finding, mixes an explanation of how the data were gathered into the results, and adds a personal opinion where the results should simply report what was found. The pieces are all there, but they are in the wrong places, so a reader cannot follow the project from question to answer. The structure is working against the writer.

{{learner-b}} lets each part do its own job. The introduction poses the question, the methodology explains how the study was done, the results report what was found without comment, and the discussion weighs what it means. A reader can follow the thread from start to finish. The structure is doing the work.

Both wrote up the same study. Only {{learner-b}} placed each piece in the part that reports it.

title: Placing each part
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these checks to see whether each part of a write-up is doing its own job.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Does the introduction set out the question and why it matters?
Does the methodology explain how the research was done, clearly enough to judge or repeat?
Do the results report what was found, without interpreting it?
Does the discussion weigh what the findings mean and how far they answer the question?
Have I kept the finding out of the introduction and opinion out of the results?
Can a reader follow the thread from question to answer?

title: Formative check: the parts of a write-up
displayTitle: Which of these lists the four core parts of a research write-up in the order they usually appear?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which lists the four core parts in the order they usually appear?

_items.text: Introduction, methodology, results, discussion.
_items.feedback: Yes. That order carries the reader from the question to what the findings mean.

_items.text: Results, introduction, discussion, methodology.
_items.feedback: The question needs to come first; results cannot open the write-up.

_items.text: Methodology, results, introduction, discussion.
_items.feedback: The introduction sets the question, so it comes before the method.

_items.text: Discussion, results, methodology, introduction.
_items.feedback: This reverses the usual order; the discussion comes last, not first.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Introduction, methodology, results, discussion carries the reader from the question to its meaning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the order that moves from question, to how, to what was found, to what it means.
_incorrect.final: The usual order is introduction, methodology, results, discussion: the question, how it was tackled, what was found, and what it means.

title: Formative check: placing the parts
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's write-up easier to follow than the first's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's write-up easier to follow?

_items.text: Each part did its own job: the question in the introduction, then the method, the findings, and their meaning.
_items.feedback: Yes. When each part does its own job, the reader can follow the thread.

_items.text: It was written in more formal, academic language.
_items.feedback: Clearer structure, not formality, is what made it easier to follow.

_items.text: It gave the main finding away in the introduction.
_items.feedback: That is what the first student did, and it confused the structure.

_items.text: It included the writer's personal opinion in the results.
_items.feedback: Opinion belongs in the discussion; in the results it muddles the parts.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student let each part do its own job, so the reader could follow the project from question to answer.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student did with the parts, rather than the style of the writing.
_incorrect.final: The second student's write-up was clearer because each part did its own job. Formality, giving the finding away early, or opinion in the results do not help the reader follow the thread.

title: Formative check: matching the part
displayTitle: You are reading a piece of {{context}} research that explains, step by step, how the study gathered its evidence. Which part are you most likely reading?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which part explains how the study gathered its evidence?

_items.text: The methodology.
_items.feedback: Yes. The methodology explains how the research was done, in {{context}} as in any subject.

_items.text: The introduction.
_items.feedback: The introduction sets out the question, not how the evidence was gathered.

_items.text: The results.
_items.feedback: The results report what was found, not how it was gathered.

_items.text: The discussion.
_items.feedback: The discussion weighs what the findings mean, not how they were gathered.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The part that explains how the evidence was gathered is the methodology.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which part explains how the research was carried out, so others could judge or repeat it?
_incorrect.final: A step-by-step account of how the evidence was gathered is the methodology. The introduction sets the question, the results report findings, and the discussion weighs their meaning.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of research writing you have read in your subject. Could you tell which part was the introduction, method, results or discussion? Which part was hardest to spot, and why?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A research write-up has a recognisable shape: introduction, methodology, results and discussion, each doing its own job. Together they carry a reader from the question, through how it was tackled, to what was found and what it means. You can now recognise the parts and tell which one a piece of writing belongs to. With what research is, how a project is shaped, and the shape it takes, you have a map of research at university.

_items.feedback: Yes. Guiding questions build the framework.

_items.text: They make the project longer and more detailed.
_items.feedback: Length is not the point of guiding questions.

_items.text: They replace the need to gather any evidence.
_items.feedback: Evidence is still needed; questions shape how you gather it.

_items.text: They prove the topic is interesting and important.
_items.feedback: Guiding questions shape the project, rather than proving interest.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Guiding questions narrow an interest into a workable framework.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about narrowing and shaping the project.

body: In a research write-up, which part explains how the research was carried out?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which part explains how the research was carried out?

_items.text: The methodology.
_items.feedback: Yes. The methodology explains how the research was done.

_items.text: The introduction.
_items.feedback: The introduction sets out the question.

_items.text: The results.
_items.feedback: The results report what was found.

_items.text: The discussion.
_items.feedback: The discussion weighs what the findings mean.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The methodology explains how the research was carried out.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which part lets someone judge or repeat the research?

body: What is the job of the discussion in a research write-up?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the job of the discussion?

_items.text: To weigh what the findings mean and how far they answer the question.
_items.feedback: Yes. The discussion weighs the meaning of the findings.

_items.text: To report what was found, without interpreting it.
_items.feedback: That is the job of the results.

_items.text: To set out the question and why it matters.
_items.feedback: That is the job of the introduction.

_items.text: To explain how the data were gathered.
_items.feedback: That is the job of the methodology.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The discussion weighs what the findings mean.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which part interprets the findings rather than reporting them?

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Research is no longer just a word for looking things up. You can explain what makes work count as research: a focused question answered with evidence towards a defensible conclusion, aiming at a fresh perspective. You can describe how a research proposal and its guiding questions shape a project into something workable. And you can recognise the main parts of a research project, introduction, methodology, results and discussion, and how they carry it from question to findings. Look back at the confidence check to see how far you have moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, research is something you will meet in every part of your degree. Each reading list is built on it, each dissertation asks for some of your own, and the habit of asking a focused question and answering it with evidence is valued well beyond university. The judgement research builds travels into professional work.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced researching courses take you into the research-document genres, such as the literature review and the report, and then into running research with rigour and ethics. Going wider: the same habits underpin Academic Writing, Finding and Using Sources, and Criticality, where you put research to work on real tasks.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what academic research is, how a research project is shaped, and the shape it takes on the page. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one connected view you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to run a research project of your own. The aim is to see these three ideas as one connected whole rather than three separate topics, so that the view carries on into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise how what research is, how a project is shaped and the shape it takes connect as one view
show the three strands working together in a worked example of a research project
plan one way to use the three strands together to make sense of research in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body: Seeing research as one connected whole means holding the three ideas together. A research project starts from a focused question, which is what makes it research. A proposal then shapes that question into a workable plan. A recognisable structure, introduction, methodology, results and discussion, carries it from question to findings. The three strands are the parts of one journey, not three separate subjects.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this connected view is something you use whenever you meet research, not a single task you finish. When you pick up an article or start a project, you look for the question, see how it has been shaped, and follow its parts to the findings. Held together, the three strands turn a daunting piece of research into something you can follow.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of research you will read in your subject this term. How could you use the three strands, the question, the shaping, and the parts of the write-up, to make sense of it? There are no right or wrong answers.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Research makes most sense when you see it as one connected whole. A focused question becomes a shaped project, and a shaped project takes a recognisable shape on the page, carrying it from question to findings. It is this connected view, not any single strand on its own, that helps you read and understand research across your studies.

title: The steps as one process
displayTitle: The steps as one process
body: A research project runs as one connected sequence, not three separate subjects. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Ask a question
_items.body: Ask a focused question - the move that turns the work into research.

_items.title: Write a proposal
_items.body: Shape that question into a workable plan by writing a proposal.

_items.title: Structure
_items.body: Set the work out in its parts - introduction, methodology, results and discussion.

_items.title: Reach findings
_items.body: Carry the project through to findings you can discuss and defend.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students read the same journal article for a seminar. One hunts only for the results, and leaves confused about what the study really showed. The other finds the question first, sees how the study was shaped and limited, and follows the method, results and discussion through to the findings. Reading research as one connected whole, the second student understands it; the three strands worked together.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to read research as one connected whole
body: Use these questions to hold the three strands together when you meet a piece of research.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Can I find the focused question the research is asking?
Can I see how the project was shaped and limited into a workable plan?
Can I name the parts of the write-up and the job each one does?
Can I follow the thread from the question through to the findings?
Can I see the three strands as one connected whole, not three separate topics?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to see the three strands as one connected whole rather than three separate topics?
body: Why is it more useful to see the three strands as one connected whole rather than three separate topics?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to see the three strands as one connected whole rather than three separate topics?

_items.text: Because each strand leads into the next: a question is shaped into a plan, and the plan sets the shape the write-up takes.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands are one journey, from question to findings.

_items.text: Because learning the parts in one list means you never have to understand any of them.
_items.feedback: Naming the parts is a start, but the point is seeing how they connect.

_items.text: Because a research project only ever has one question and nothing else matters.
_items.feedback: A project has a question, a plan and a structure, which is why the strands connect.

_items.text: Because the three strands have nothing to do with each other.
_items.feedback: They are closely connected, since each one leads into the next.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Seeing the strands as one journey helps you make sense of research from question to findings.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how a question, a plan and a structure connect into one journey.

displayTitle: A student reads a journal article. They spot the focused question in the introduction, notice how the study was shaped and limited, and follow the method, results and discussion through to the findings. What does this show?
body: A student reads a journal article. They spot the focused question in the introduction, notice how the study was shaped and limited, and follow the method, results and discussion through to the findings. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student reads a journal article. They spot the focused question in the introduction, notice how the study was shaped and limited, and follow the method, results and discussion through to the findings. What does this show?

_items.text: That they are reading research as one connected whole, using the three strands together to follow it from question to findings.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands worked together as one view of the whole project.

_items.text: That the article was too simple to count as real research.
_items.feedback: Spotting the parts does not make the research simple; it shows the strands working together.

_items.text: That only the introduction matters when you read research.
_items.feedback: Each part did a job here, not just the introduction.

_items.text: That the student was only interested in the final results.
_items.feedback: They followed the whole thread, from the question through to the findings.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading with the three strands together lets you follow a whole project, from its question to what its findings mean.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the student used all three strands to follow the whole article.

displayTitle: You want to use this connected view to make sense of research in {{context}} this term. Which plan best brings the three strands together?
body: You want to use this connected view to make sense of research in {{context}} this term. Which plan best brings the three strands together?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this connected view to make sense of research in your subject this term. Which plan best brings the three strands together?

_items.text: When you meet a piece of research, find its question, see how it was shaped, and follow its parts through to the findings.
_items.feedback: Yes. That uses all three strands together as one connected view.

_items.text: Read only the results of each study and skip the question and the method.
_items.feedback: The results make little sense without the question and the method behind them.

_items.text: Memorise the four part names and never look at an actual study.
_items.feedback: Naming the parts helps only when you use it on real research.

_items.text: Decide a study is research only if it is about a topic you already like.
_items.feedback: What makes work research is its question and evidence, not whether you like the topic.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Finding the question, seeing the shaping, and following the parts brings the three strands together on real research.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan uses all three strands on a real piece of research.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What does it mean to see research as one connected whole?
body: What does it mean to see research as one connected whole?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to see research as one connected whole?

_items.text: Holding together what research is, how it is shaped, and the shape it takes, as one journey from question to findings.
_items.feedback: Yes. One journey, made of the three strands.

_items.text: Treating the question, the proposal and the write-up as three unrelated topics.
_items.feedback: The three strands are connected, not unrelated.

_items.text: Focusing only on the final results of a study.
_items.feedback: The results make sense only alongside the question and the method.

_items.text: Deciding that only a dissertation counts as real research.
_items.feedback: Research is defined by a question and evidence, not by its length.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student meets an unfamiliar study. They find its question, see how it was shaped and limited, and follow its parts to the findings. What are they doing?
body: A student meets an unfamiliar study. They find its question, see how it was shaped and limited, and follow its parts to the findings. What are they doing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student meets an unfamiliar study. They find its question, see how it was shaped and limited, and follow its parts to the findings. What are they doing?

_items.text: Bringing the three strands together to read the study as one connected whole.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three strands, used together.

_items.text: Judging the study only by how long it is.
_items.feedback: Length does not make something research.

_items.text: Reading the discussion first and ignoring the rest.
_items.feedback: They followed the whole thread, not one part.

_items.text: Deciding the study is too hard to understand.
_items.feedback: Using the three strands is what made it understandable.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
